nodes.name: Hermes' Lipschitz/continuous selector theorem
nodes.statement: In contrast to this, it was shown in \cite{Hermes} that a Lipschitz continuous multifunction $F$ on $[a,b]$ with compact images from $\mathbb{R}^N$ admits a Lipschitz continuous selector, whose Lipschitz constant does not exceed that of the multifunction; furthermore, if $F$ is only continuous and of bounded (Jordan) variation, then it admits a \emph{continuous\/} selector.
assumptions: a Lipschitz continuous multifunction $F$ on $[a,b]$ with compact images from $\mathbb{R}^N$
if $F$ is only continuous and of bounded (Jordan) variation
conclusions: admits a Lipschitz continuous selector, whose Lipschitz constant does not exceed that of the multifunction
it admits a \emph{continuous\/} selector
nodes.statement_short: Lipschitz compact-valued multifunctions on $[a,b]$ into $\mathbb{R}^N$ have Lipschitz selectors; continuous BV ones have continuous selectors.

nodes.name: Selector of bounded variation through a given point (Banach-space values)
nodes.statement: Changing the compactness arguments to generalized Helly's pointwise selection principle, it was proved in \cite{JDCS} that a multifunction $F$ on $[a,b]$ of bounded Jordan variation with compact images from a Banach space admits a selector, whose total Jordan variation does not exceed that of $F$ and passes through a given point in the graph of~$F$.
assumptions: a multifunction $F$ on $[a,b]$ of bounded Jordan variation with compact images from a Banach space
conclusions: admits a selector, whose total Jordan variation does not exceed that of $F$ and passes through a given point in the graph of~$F$
nodes.statement_short: A compact-valued BV multifunction into a Banach space has a selector with no larger variation through any point of its graph.

nodes.name: Metric space $(M,d)$
nodes.statement: Throughout the paper $(M,d)$ is a metric space with metric $d$.

nodes.name: Pompeiu excess
nodes.statement: Given two nonempty sets $X,Y\subset M$, the \emph{Pompeiu excess\/} ({\it {\'e}cart}, in French) {\it of $X$ over $Y$} is defined by (\cite[pp.~281--282]{Pomp}, \cite[Chapter~II]{CV}) \begin{equation*} e(X,Y)\equiv e_d(X,Y):=\sup_{x\in X}d(x,Y)=\inf\{r>0:X\subset\mathcal{O}_r(Y)\}, \end{equation*} where $d(x,Y):=\inf_{y\in Y}d(x,y)$ is the distance\footnote{$d(x,\varnothing):=+\infty.$} from $x\in M$ to $Y$, and the set $\mathcal{O}_r(Y):=\{x\in M:d(x,Y)<r\}$ is the open $r$-neighbourhood \footnote{$\mathcal{O}_r(\varnothing)\!:=\!\varnothing$ for $r>0$; $e(\varnothing,Y):=0$ for any $Y\subset M$, and $e(X,\varnothing):=+\infty$ if $\varnothing\!\ne\! X\!\subset\! M$.} of~$Y$, $r>0$ (if $Y=\{y\}$, $\mathcal{O}_r(y)\equiv\mathcal{O}_r(Y)$ is simply the open ball of radius $r$ centered at $y\in M$).
nodes.statement_short: The excess $e(X,Y)=\sup_{x\in X}d(x,Y)$ of $X$ over $Y$, with distance to a set and open $r$-neighbourhoods.

nodes.name: Properties of the Pompeiu excess
nodes.statement: The well-known properties of $e(\cdot,\cdot)$ are as follows. Given $X,Y,Z\subset M$: \par\vspace{2pt} (a) $e(X,Y)\!=\!0$ iff\footnote{`iff' means as usual `if and only if'.} $X\!\subset\!\ov{Y}$, where $\ov{Y}\!=\!\bigcap_{r>0}\mathcal{O}_r(Y)$ is the closure of $Y$~in~$M$; \par\vspace{2pt} (b) $e(X,Y)\le e(X,Z)+e(Z,Y)$ (triangle inequality for~$e$); \par\vspace{2pt} (c) $e(X,Y)<+\infty$ provided $X$ and $Y$ are bounded (and, in particular bounded and closed, or compact).
assumptions: Given $X,Y,Z\subset M$:
conclusions: $e(X,Y)\le e(X,Z)+e(Z,Y)$ (triangle inequality for~$e$)
$e(X,Y)<+\infty$ provided $X$ and $Y$ are bounded
nodes.statement_short: Excess vanishes iff $X\subset\overline{Y}$, satisfies the triangle inequality, and is finite on bounded sets.

nodes.name: Pompeiu-Hausdorff distance
nodes.statement: The \emph{Pompeiu-Hausdorff distance\/} between two sets $X,Y\subset M$ is defined by (e.g., \cite{Pomp}, \cite[Chapter~II]{CV}) \footnote{Pompeiu \cite{Pomp} symmetrized the excess $e$ by $d_P(X,Y)\!:=\!e(X,Y)\!+\!e(Y,X)$ (cf. also~\cite{Ber-Pac}).} \begin{equation*} d_H(X,Y)\!:=\max\{e(X,Y),e(Y,X)\}\!=\! \inf\{r\!>\!0:\mbox{$X\!\subset\!\mathcal{O}_r(Y)$\,and\,$Y\!\subset\!\mathcal{O}_r(X)$}\}. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: $d_H$ is a metric on bcl$(M)$ and c$(M)$
nodes.statement: It follows from (a), (b), and (c) above that $d_H$ is a \emph{metric\/} (with finite values), called the \emph{Pompeiu-Hausdorff metric}, on the family $\mbox{bcl}(M)$ of all nonempty \emph{bounded closed\/} subsets of $M$ and, in particular on the family $\mbox{c}(M)$ of all nonempty \emph{compact\/} subsets of~$M$.
assumptions: It follows from (a), (b), and (c) above
conclusions: $d_H$ is a \emph{metric\/} (with finite values), called the \emph{Pompeiu-Hausdorff metric}, on the family $\mbox{bcl}(M)$ of all nonempty \emph{bounded closed\/} subsets of $M$
nodes.statement_short: $d_H$ is a finite metric on nonempty bounded closed sets bcl$(M)$, in particular on nonempty compact sets c$(M)$.

nodes.name: Multifunction (set-valued mapping)
nodes.statement: A \emph{multifunction\/} (or \emph{set-valued mapping\/}) from a nonempty set $T$ into $M$ is a rule $F$, which assigns to each $t\in T$ a unique subset $F(t)\subset M$; in symbols, $F:T\to\mathcal{P}(M)$, where $\mathcal{P}(M)$ is the power set of $M$ (=\,the family of all subsets of~$M$).
differentia: assigns to each $t\in T$ a unique subset $F(t)\subset M$

nodes.name: Set-valued selector
nodes.statement: A multifunction $\Gamma:T\to\mathcal{P}(M)$ is said to be a \emph{set-valued selector\/} of $F:T\to\mathcal{P}(M)$ on $T$ provided $\Gamma(t)\subset F(t)$ for all $t\in T$.

nodes.name: Selector (selection)
nodes.statement: If $\Gamma:T\to M$ is single-valued and $\Gamma(t)\in F(t)$ for all $t\in T$, then $\Gamma$ is called a \emph{selector\/} (or \emph{selection\/}) of~$F$ on~$T$.

nodes.name: Jordan variation; bounded variation of a multifunction
nodes.statement: Of main interest in this paper are multifunctions $F:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$ with $T$ a nonempty subset of the reals $\mathbb{R}$. Such an $F$ is said to be \emph{of bounded variation\/} (with respect to~$d_H$) provided its (total) \emph{Jordan variation\/} \begin{equation*} \mbox{\rm V}(F,T)\!:=\sup_\pi\sum_{i=1}^m d_H\bigl(F(t_{i-1}),F(t_i)\bigr)\quad \mbox{is finite\quad ($\mbox{\rm V}(F,\varnothing):=0$),} \end{equation*} the supremum being taken over all partitions $\pi$ of the set $T\subset\mathbb{R}$, i.e., $m\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\pi=\{t_i\}_{i=0}^m\subset T$ such that $t_{i-1}\le t_i$ for all $i\in\{1,\dots,m\}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathrm{V}(F,T)$ is the sup over partitions of $\sum d_H(F(t_{i-1}),F(t_i))$; $F$ is of bounded variation if it is finite.

nodes.name: Theorem A (set-valued selectors of bounded variation)
nodes.statement: Given $T\subset\mathbb{R}$, $t_0\in T$, $X_0\in\mbox{\rm c}(M)$, and $F:T\to\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ such that $\mbox{\rm V}(F,T)<+\infty$, there exists a set-valued selector $\Gamma:T\to\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ of $F$ on $T$ such that $d_H(X_0,\Gamma(t_0))\le e(X_0,F(t_0))$ and\/ $\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T)\le\mbox{\rm V}(F,T)$. {\rm(}In particular, if $X_0\subset F(t_0)$, the first inequality above gives $\Gamma(t_0)=X_0$.{\rm)} Furthermore, if $x_0\in M$ and $X_0=\{x_0\}$, then $\Gamma:T\to M$ may be chosen to be single-valued and such that $d(x_0,\Gamma(t_0))\le d(x_0,F(t_0))$.
assumptions: Given $T\subset\mathbb{R}$, $t_0\in T$, $X_0\in\mbox{\rm c}(M)$, and $F:T\to\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ such that $\mbox{\rm V}(F,T)<+\infty$
conclusions: there exists a set-valued selector $\Gamma:T\to\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ of $F$ on $T$ such that $d_H(X_0,\Gamma(t_0))\le e(X_0,F(t_0))$ and\/ $\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T)\le\mbox{\rm V}(F,T)$
then $\Gamma:T\to M$ may be chosen to be single-valued and such that $d(x_0,\Gamma(t_0))\le d(x_0,F(t_0))$
nodes.statement_short: A compact-valued multifunction of bounded variation has a set-valued selector through prescribed initial data with no larger variation.
nodes.label: t:A

nodes.name: Directional (excess) variations to the right and to the left
nodes.statement: In order to do it, given $F:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$, following \cite{JMAA07} the quantities \begin{equation*} {\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)\!:=\!\sup_\pi\sum_{i=1}^m e\bigl(F(t_{i-1}\!),F(t_i)\bigr) \mbox{ and \,} {\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)\!:=\!\sup_\pi\sum_{i=1}^m e\bigl(F(t_i),F(t_{i-1}\!)\bigr) \end{equation*} are said to be the \emph{directional\/} (or \emph{excess\/}) \emph{variations of $F$ to the right\/} and \emph{to the left}, respectively (${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,\varnothing)={\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,\varnothing):=0$).
nodes.statement_short: Right/left variations: sup over partitions of sums of excesses $e(F(t_{i-1}),F(t_i))$, resp. $e(F(t_i),F(t_{i-1}))$.

nodes.name: Comparison of Jordan and directional variations
nodes.statement: Clearly, \begin{equation*} \max\bigl\{{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T),{\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)\bigr\}\le\mbox{\rm V}(F,T)\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)+{\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T), \end{equation*} and so, $\mbox{\rm V}(F,T)$ is finite iff both ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)$ and ${\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)$ are finite.
conclusions: $\mbox{\rm V}(F,T)$ is finite iff both ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)$ and ${\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)$ are finite
nodes.statement_short: $\max(\vec V,\overleftarrow V)\le V\le \vec V+\overleftarrow V$, so $V$ is finite iff both directional variations are.

nodes.name: Notation $T_S$
nodes.statement: For brevity, we write $T_S:=T\cap S$ for $S\subset\mathbb{R}$ (e.g., $T_{[t_0,+\infty)}=T\cap[t_0,+\infty)$ for $t_0\in T$, etc.).

nodes.name: Zero variation iff constant
nodes.statement: By the definition of $\mbox{\rm V}$, $\mbox{\rm V}(F,T)=0$ iff $F$ is constant on $T$.
conclusions: $\mbox{\rm V}(F,T)=0$ iff $F$ is constant on $T$

nodes.name: Zero right variation iff nondecreasing
nodes.statement: The definition of~${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}$ and property (a) of $e$ in Section~\ref{s:mr} imply ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)=0$ iff $F$ is \emph{nondecreasing\/} on $T$ in the sense that $F(s)\subset F(t)$ for all $s,t\in T$ with $s\le t$.
conclusions: ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)=0$ iff $F$ is \emph{nondecreasing\/} on $T$
nodes.statement_short: $\vec V(F,T)=0$ iff $F$ is nondecreasing ($F(s)\subset F(t)$ for $s\le t$).

nodes.name: Zero left variation iff nonincreasing
nodes.statement: Similarly, ${\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)=0$ iff $F$ is \emph{nonincresing\/} on $T$, i.e., $F(s)\supset F(t)$ for all $s,t\in T$,~$s\le t$.
conclusions: iff $F$ is \emph{nonincresing\/} on $T$

nodes.name: Additivity of the Jordan variation
nodes.statement: Since $(\mbox{c}(M),d_H)$ is a metric space, it is known (e.g., \cite[2.19]{Var}, \cite{JDCS}, \cite{MatSb}) that $\mbox{\rm V}$ is \emph{additive\/} (in the second variable) in the sense that \begin{equation} \mbox{\rm V}(F,T)=\mbox{\rm V}(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})+\mbox{\rm V}(F,T_{[t,+\infty)})\quad\mbox{for all \,\,$t\in T$.} \end{equation}
assumptions: Since $(\mbox{c}(M),d_H)$ is a metric space
conclusions: $\mbox{\rm V}$ is \emph{additive\/} (in the second variable)
nodes.statement_short: $V(F,T)=V(F,T\cap(-\infty,t])+V(F,T\cap[t,\infty))$ for all $t\in T$.

nodes.name: Additivity identity (e:Vadd)
nodes.statement: \mbox{\rm V}(F,T)=\mbox{\rm V}(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})+\mbox{\rm V}(F,T_{[t,+\infty)})\quad\mbox{for all \,\,$t\in T$.}
nodes.label: e:Vadd

nodes.name: Additivity of directional variations
nodes.statement: We assert that the additivity property \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Vadd})} holds also for ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}$ and ${\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}$ in place of~$\mbox{\rm V}$.
conclusions: the additivity property \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Vadd})} holds also for ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}$ and ${\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}$
nodes.statement_short: The additivity identity holds for the right and left directional variations.

nodes.name: Proof of additivity of the right variation
nodes.statement: Given $\xi,\eta\in\mathbb{R}$ such that $\xi<{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})$ and $\eta<{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t,+\infty)})$, there are $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$, a partition $\{t_i\}_{i=0}^m$ of $T_{(-\infty,t]}$ with $t_m=t$ and a partition $\{s_j\}_{j=0}^n$ of $T_{[t,+\infty)}$ with $s_0=t$ such that \begin{equation} \xi<\sum_{i=1}^m e(F(t_{i-1}),F(t_i))\quad\mbox{and}\quad \eta<\sum_{j=1}^n e(F(s_{j-1}),F(s_j)). \end{equation} Since $\{t_i\}_{i=0}^m\cup\{s_j\}_{j=0}^n$ is a partition of $T$, we get, from \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:xi1})}, $\xi+\eta<{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)$, which, due to the arbitrariness of $\xi$ and $\eta$ as above, implies the inequality \begin{equation*} {\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})+{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t,+\infty)})\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T). \end{equation*} In order to prove the reverse inequality, let $\xi\in\mathbb{R}$ be arbitrary such that $\xi<{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)$. Then, there are $m\in\mathbb{N}$ and a partition $\pi=\{t_i\}_{i=0}^m$ of $T$ such that the first inequality in \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:xi1})} holds. If $t_m\le t$, then $\pi$ is a partition of $T_{(-\infty,t]}$, and if $t\le t_0$, then $\pi$ is a partition of $T_{[t,+\infty)}$, and so, in the either case, the first inequality in \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:xi1})} implies \begin{equation} \xi<{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})+{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t,+\infty)}). \end{equation} Now, suppose $t_{k-1}\le t\le t_k$ for some $k\in\{1,\dots,m\}$. By the triangle inequality for~$e$, we have \begin{equation} e(F(t_{k-1}),F(t_k))\le e(F(t_{k-1}),F(t))+e(F(t),F(t_k)). \end{equation} Since $\{t_i\}_{i=0}^{k-1}\cup\{t\}$ is a partition of $T_{(-\infty,t]}$ and $\{t\}\cup\{t_i\}_{i=k}^m$ is a partition of $T_{[t,+\infty)}$, from the first inequality in \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:xi1})} and \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:kk})}, once again we get \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:x2})}. By the arbitrariness of $\xi<{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)$, \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:x2})} implies \begin{equation*} {\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})+{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t,+\infty)}), \end{equation*} which was to be proved. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Two inequalities via partitions: concatenate partitions for $\ge$; insert $t$ into a partition using the excess triangle inequality for $\le$.

nodes.name: Partition sums exceed $\xi,\eta$ (e:xi1)
nodes.statement: \xi<\sum_{i=1}^m e(F(t_{i-1}),F(t_i))\quad\mbox{and}\quad \eta<\sum_{j=1}^n e(F(s_{j-1}),F(s_j)).
nodes.label: e:xi1

nodes.name: Bound (e:x2)
nodes.statement: \xi<{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})+{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t,+\infty)}).
nodes.label: e:x2

nodes.name: Choose near-optimal partitions
nodes.statement: Given $\xi,\eta\in\mathbb{R}$ such that $\xi<{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})$ and $\eta<{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t,+\infty)})$, there are $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$, a partition $\{t_i\}_{i=0}^m$ of $T_{(-\infty,t]}$ with $t_m=t$ and a partition $\{s_j\}_{j=0}^n$ of $T_{[t,+\infty)}$ with $s_0=t$ such that \begin{equation} \xi<\sum_{i=1}^m e(F(t_{i-1}),F(t_i))\quad\mbox{and}\quad \eta<\sum_{j=1}^n e(F(s_{j-1}),F(s_j)). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Choose partitions of both halves whose excess sums exceed $\xi,\eta$.

nodes.name: Concatenate to get superadditivity
nodes.statement: Since $\{t_i\}_{i=0}^m\cup\{s_j\}_{j=0}^n$ is a partition of $T$, we get, from \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:xi1})}, $\xi+\eta<{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)$, which, due to the arbitrariness of $\xi$ and $\eta$ as above, implies the inequality \begin{equation*} {\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})+{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t,+\infty)})\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Union of partitions is a partition of $T$, giving $\vec V$ of halves summed $\le\vec V(F,T)$.

nodes.name: Setup for reverse inequality
nodes.statement: In order to prove the reverse inequality, let $\xi\in\mathbb{R}$ be arbitrary such that $\xi<{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)$. Then, there are $m\in\mathbb{N}$ and a partition $\pi=\{t_i\}_{i=0}^m$ of $T$ such that the first inequality in \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:xi1})} holds.
nodes.statement_short: Take a partition of $T$ with excess sum exceeding $\xi$.

nodes.name: Case: partition on one side of $t$
nodes.statement: If $t_m\le t$, then $\pi$ is a partition of $T_{(-\infty,t]}$, and if $t\le t_0$, then $\pi$ is a partition of $T_{[t,+\infty)}$, and so, in the either case, the first inequality in \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:xi1})} implies \begin{equation} \xi<{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})+{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t,+\infty)}). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: If the partition lies on one side of $t$, the bound (e:x2) is immediate.

nodes.name: Case: $t$ inside a partition interval
nodes.statement: Now, suppose $t_{k-1}\le t\le t_k$ for some $k\in\{1,\dots,m\}$. By the triangle inequality for~$e$, we have \begin{equation} e(F(t_{k-1}),F(t_k))\le e(F(t_{k-1}),F(t))+e(F(t),F(t_k)). \end{equation} Since $\{t_i\}_{i=0}^{k-1}\cup\{t\}$ is a partition of $T_{(-\infty,t]}$ and $\{t\}\cup\{t_i\}_{i=k}^m$ is a partition of $T_{[t,+\infty)}$, from the first inequality in \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:xi1})} and \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:kk})}, once again we get \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:x2})}.
nodes.statement_short: Insert $t$ using the triangle inequality for $e$ to get (e:x2).

nodes.name: Conclude subadditivity
nodes.statement: By the arbitrariness of $\xi<{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)$, \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:x2})} implies \begin{equation*} {\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})+{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t,+\infty)}), \end{equation*} which was to be proved. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Arbitrariness of $\xi$ gives the reverse inequality.

nodes.name: Variation function $v_F$
nodes.statement: Recall that the function $v_F(t)\!:=\!\mbox{\rm V}(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})$, $t\!\in\! T$, is said to be the {\it var\-i\-a\-tion function\/} of $F$ on~$T$.

nodes.name: Variation functions to the right and to the left
nodes.statement: We define the \emph{variation function\/} of $F$ to the right (to the left) by $\ori{v}_F(t):={\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})$ (by $\ole{v}_F(t):={\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})$, respectively) for all $t\in T$.
nodes.definiendum: variation function of $F$ to the right (to the left)

nodes.name: Variation functions are nondecreasing
nodes.statement: Clearly, $v_F,\ori{v}_F,\ole{v}_F:T\to[0,+\infty]$ are \emph{nondecreasing\/} on~$T$.
conclusions: $v_F,\ori{v}_F,\ole{v}_F:T\to[0,+\infty]$ are \emph{nondecreasing\/} on~$T$

nodes.name: Characterization of bounded right variation
nodes.statement: Given $F:T\to\mbox{\rm c}(M)$, ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)<+\infty$ iff there is a nondecreasing bounded function $\varphi:T\to\mathbb{R}$ such that $e(F(s),F(t))\le\varphi(t)-\varphi(s)$ for all $s,t\in T$ with $s\le t;$ moreover, ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)\le\mbox{\rm V}(\varphi,T)$. {\rm(}A similar assertion holds for ${\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)<+\infty$ if the inequality is written as $e(F(t),F(s))\le\varphi(t)-\varphi(s)$.{\rm)}
assumptions: Given $F:T\to\mbox{\rm c}(M)$
conclusions: there is a nondecreasing bounded function $\varphi:T\to\mathbb{R}$ such that $e(F(s),F(t))\le\varphi(t)-\varphi(s)$ for all $s,t\in T$ with $s\le t;$
nodes.statement_short: $\vec V(F,T)<\infty$ iff the excess is dominated by increments of a bounded nondecreasing $\varphi$; then $\vec V(F,T)\le V(\varphi,T)$.
nodes.label: l:char

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: ($\Rightarrow\!$) Let $\ori{v}(t)={\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})$, $t\in T$, be the variation function (to the right) of~$F$. It is nondecreasing on $T$ and bounded: $\sup_{t\in T}\ori{v}(t)\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)$. Given $s,t\in T$, $s\le t$, the additivity of ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}$ implies \begin{equation*} e(F(s),F(t))\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[s,t]})={\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})-{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(-\infty,s]}) =\ori{v}(t)-\ori{v}(s). \end{equation*} It remains to set $\varphi:=\ori{v}$. ($\!\Leftarrow$) Let $m\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\pi=\{t_i\}_{i=0}^m$ be a partition of $T$. Since $t_{i-1}\le t_i$ for all $i=1,\dots,m$, by the assumption we get \begin{align*} \sum_{i=1}^me(F(t_{i-1}),F(t_i))&\le\sum_{i=1}^m\bigl(\varphi(t_i)-\varphi(t_{i-1})\bigr) =\varphi(t_m)-\varphi(t_0)\\ &\le\sup_{t\in T}\varphi(t)-\inf_{s\in T}\varphi(s)=\mbox{\rm V}(\varphi,T)<+\infty. \end{align*} It remains to take the supremum over all partitions $\pi$ of $T$. \qed
nodes.statement_short: ($\Rightarrow$) take $\varphi$ the right variation function, using additivity; ($\Leftarrow$) telescope the bound over partitions.

nodes.name: Necessity: take $\varphi$ the right variation function
nodes.statement: ($\Rightarrow\!$) Let $\ori{v}(t)={\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})$, $t\in T$, be the variation function (to the right) of~$F$. It is nondecreasing on $T$ and bounded: $\sup_{t\in T}\ori{v}(t)\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)$. Given $s,t\in T$, $s\le t$, the additivity of ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}$ implies \begin{equation*} e(F(s),F(t))\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[s,t]})={\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})-{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(-\infty,s]}) =\ori{v}(t)-\ori{v}(s). \end{equation*} It remains to set $\varphi:=\ori{v}$.
nodes.statement_short: Additivity of $\vec V$ shows $\varphi=\vec v$ works.

nodes.name: Sufficiency: telescope over partitions
nodes.statement: ($\!\Leftarrow$) Let $m\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\pi=\{t_i\}_{i=0}^m$ be a partition of $T$. Since $t_{i-1}\le t_i$ for all $i=1,\dots,m$, by the assumption we get \begin{align*} \sum_{i=1}^me(F(t_{i-1}),F(t_i))&\le\sum_{i=1}^m\bigl(\varphi(t_i)-\varphi(t_{i-1})\bigr) =\varphi(t_m)-\varphi(t_0)\\ &\le\sup_{t\in T}\varphi(t)-\inf_{s\in T}\varphi(s)=\mbox{\rm V}(\varphi,T)<+\infty. \end{align*} It remains to take the supremum over all partitions $\pi$ of $T$. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Excess sums telescope to at most $V(\varphi,T)$.

nodes.name: Total boundedness of the image fails under bounded directional variation
nodes.statement: It is known (\cite[1.23]{Var}, \cite[Lemma~11]{MZ}) that if $F:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$ and $\mbox{\rm V}(F,T)\!<\!+\infty$, then the image $F(T):=\bigcup_{t\in T}F(t)$ is a \emph{totally bounded\/} (hence separable) subset of~$M$ (if, in addition, $(M,d)$ is complete, then the closure of $F(T)$ in $M$ is compact). However, condition $\mbox{\rm V}(F,T)\!<\!+\infty$ cannot be replaced neither by ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)\!<\!+\infty$ nor by ${\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)\!<\!+\infty$ (see Example~\ref{ex:5.5}).
nodes.statement_short: Finite Jordan variation makes $F(T)$ totally bounded, but finite directional variation does not.
nodes.label: p:7

nodes.name: Lower semicontinuity of the Jordan variation
nodes.statement: If a sequence $\{F_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ of multifunctions $F_n:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$ \emph{converges in $\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ pointwise on $T$} to $F$ (i.e., $d_H(F_n(t),F(t))\to0$ as $n\to\infty$ for all $t\in T$), then \begin{equation} \mbox{\rm V}(F,T)\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\mbox{\rm V}(F_n,T). \end{equation} This property is known as the (sequential) \emph{lower semicontinuity\/} of~$\mbox{\rm V}$ (in the first variable) for metric space valued functions; cf. \cite[Proposition~2.1(V7)]{MatSb}.
assumptions: If a sequence $\{F_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ of multifunctions $F_n:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$ \emph{converges in $\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ pointwise on $T$} to $F$
nodes.statement_short: Pointwise $d_H$-limits satisfy $V(F,T)\le\liminf V(F_n,T)$.

nodes.name: Lower semicontinuity inequality (e:Vsem)
nodes.statement: \mbox{\rm V}(F,T)\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\mbox{\rm V}(F_n,T).
nodes.label: e:Vsem

nodes.name: Lower semicontinuity of directional variations
nodes.statement: We assert that \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Vsem})} is valid for ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}$ and ${\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}$ in place of $\mbox{\rm V}$, as well.
nodes.statement_short: The lower semicontinuity inequality holds for $\vec V$ and $\overleftarrow V$.

nodes.name: Proof of lower semicontinuity of the right variation
nodes.statement: For any $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $s,t\in T$, the triangle inequality for $e$ implies \begin{equation*} |e(F_n(s),F_n(t))-e(F(s),F(t))|\le d_H(F_n(s),F(s))+d_H(F_n(t),F(t)), \end{equation*} and so, by the pointwise convergence of $F_n$ to $F$, $e(F_n(s),F_n(t))\!\to\! e(F(s),F(t))$ as $n\to\infty$. Given $m\in\mathbb{N}$ and a partition $\pi=\{t_i\}_{i=0}^m$ of $T$, by definition of~${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}$, \begin{equation*} \sum_{i=1}^m e(F_n(t_{i-1}),F_n(t_i))\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F_n,T)\quad\mbox{for all \,\,$n\in\mathbb{N}$.} \end{equation*} Passing to the limit inferior as $n\to\infty$, we get \begin{equation*} \sum_{i=1}^m e(F(t_{i-1}),F(t_i))\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F_n,T), \end{equation*} and it remains to take the supremum over all partitions $\pi$ of $T$. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Excesses converge under pointwise $d_H$ convergence; pass to liminf in partition sums and take the supremum.

nodes.name: Excesses converge
nodes.statement: For any $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $s,t\in T$, the triangle inequality for $e$ implies \begin{equation*} |e(F_n(s),F_n(t))-e(F(s),F(t))|\le d_H(F_n(s),F(s))+d_H(F_n(t),F(t)), \end{equation*} and so, by the pointwise convergence of $F_n$ to $F$, $e(F_n(s),F_n(t))\!\to\! e(F(s),F(t))$ as $n\to\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Triangle inequality for $e$ gives convergence of excesses.

nodes.name: Partition sums bounded by $\vec V(F_n,T)$
nodes.statement: Given $m\in\mathbb{N}$ and a partition $\pi=\{t_i\}_{i=0}^m$ of $T$, by definition of~${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}$, \begin{equation*} \sum_{i=1}^m e(F_n(t_{i-1}),F_n(t_i))\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F_n,T)\quad\mbox{for all \,\,$n\in\mathbb{N}$.} \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Each partition sum for $F_n$ is at most $\vec V(F_n,T)$.

nodes.name: Pass to liminf and supremum
nodes.statement: Passing to the limit inferior as $n\to\infty$, we get \begin{equation*} \sum_{i=1}^m e(F(t_{i-1}),F(t_i))\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F_n,T), \end{equation*} and it remains to take the supremum over all partitions $\pi$ of $T$. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Take liminf, then sup over partitions.

nodes.name: Limit equalities for directional variations
nodes.statement: We are going to show that these assertions hold for ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}$ and ${\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}$ as well.
nodes.statement_short: The limit equalities hold for $\vec V$ and $\overleftarrow V$.

nodes.statement:
Since $\ori{v}$ is nondecreasing on $T$, the limit on the right in \mbox{m(ef{e:ttos})} (with $\mbox{m V}$ replaced by~${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{m V}}}$) exists in $[0,+\infty]$ and is equal to $\sup_{t\in T}\ori{v}(t)$. nodes.name: Limit exists as supremum
nodes.statement: Since $\ori{v}$ is nondecreasing on $T$, the limit on the right in \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:ttos})} (with $\mbox{\rm V}$ replaced by~${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}$) exists in $[0,+\infty]$ and is equal to $\sup_{t\in T}\ori{v}(t)$.
nodes.statement_short: The limit exists by monotonicity of $\vec v$.

nodes.name: Upper bound
nodes.statement: Given $t\in T$, we have $T_{(-\infty,t]}\subset T$, and so, $\ori{v}(t)\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)$, which implies $\lim_{T\ni t\to s}\ori{v}(t)\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)$.
nodes.statement_short: $\vec v(t)\le\vec V(F,T)$, so the limit is at most $\vec V(F,T)$.

nodes.name: Lower bound via partitions
nodes.statement: Conversely, given $\xi\in\mathbb{R}$ with $\xi<{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)$, there are $m\in\mathbb{N}$ and a partition $\pi=\{t_i\}_{i=0}^m$ of $T$ (and so, \mbox{$t_0\le t_1\le\dots\le t_{m-1}\le t_m<s$}) such that \begin{equation*} \xi<\sum_{i=1}^m e(F(t_{i-1}),F(t_i))\le\ori{v}(t_m)\le\lim_{T\ni t\to s}\ori{v}(t). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: A near-optimal partition lies below $s$, bounding $\xi$ by the limit.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Passing to the limit as $\xi\to{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)$, we get ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)\le\lim_{T\ni t\to s}\ori{v}(t)$. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Let $\xi\to\vec V(F,T)$.

nodes.name: Left (right) limit point of $T$
nodes.statement: We say that $t\in\mathbb{R}$ is a \emph{left\/} (\emph{right\/}) \emph{limit point\/} of~$T$ if $T_{(t-\varepsilon,t)}\ne\varnothing$ (respectively, $T_{(t,t+\varepsilon)}\ne\varnothing$) for all $\varepsilon>0$.

nodes.name: Left (right) isolated point of $T$
nodes.statement: A point $t\in T$, which is not a left (or right) limit point of $T$, is called the \emph{left\/} (or \emph{right\/}) \emph{isolated point\/} of~$T$.
differentia: not a left (or right) limit point of $T$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3
nodes.statement: As in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:jumps}, we concentrate on ($\ori{\mbox{\rm a}}$) and ($\ori{\mbox{\rm b}}$). nodes.name: Modulus of variation
nodes.statement: Given $F:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$, its \emph{modulus of variation\/} is the nondecreasing sequence $\{\nu_k(F,T)\}_{k=1}^\infty\subset[0,+\infty]$ defined by \begin{equation*} \nu_k(F,T)\!:=\sup\,\sum_{i=1}^k d_H(F(s_i),F(t_i)), \end{equation*} the supremum being taken over all collections $s_1,\dots,s_k,t_1\dots,t_k$ of $2k$ numbers from $T$ such that $s_1\le t_1\le s_2\le t_2\le\dots\le s_{k-1}\le t_{k-1} \le s_k\le t_k$.
nodes.statement_short: $\nu_k(F,T)$ is the sup of $\sum_{i=1}^k d_H(F(s_i),F(t_i))$ over $k$ non-overlapping ordered pairs.

nodes.name: Modulus of variation bounds and converges to the variation
nodes.statement: The general case of metric space valued functions was considered in \cite{JMAA05}, whence we know that $\nu_k(F,T)\le\mbox{\rm V}(F,T)$ for all $k\in\mathbb{N}$, and $\nu_k(F,T)\to\mbox{\rm V}(F,T)$ as $k\to\infty$.
conclusions: $\nu_k(F,T)\le\mbox{\rm V}(F,T)$ for all $k\in\mathbb{N}$
$\nu_k(F,T)\to\mbox{\rm V}(F,T)$ as $k\to\infty$

nodes.name: Pointwise selection principle (Theorem B)
nodes.statement: Suppose $\{F_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ is a sequence of multifunctions $F_n:T\to\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ such that\/ {\rm(a)} $\limsup_{n\to\infty}\nu_k(F_n,T)=o(k)$ \footnote{Equality $\mu_k=o(k)$ means as usual that $\lim_{k\to\infty}\mu_k/k=0$.}, and\/ {\rm(b)}~the closure in $\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ of the set $\{F_n(t):n\in\mathbb{N}\}$ is compact for all $t\in T$. Then $\{F_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ admits a subsequence, which converges in $\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ pointwise on $T$ to a multifunction $F:T\to\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ such that $\nu_k(F,T)=o(k)$.
assumptions: {\rm(a)} $\limsup_{n\to\infty}\nu_k(F_n,T)=o(k)$
{\rm(b)}~the closure in $\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ of the set $\{F_n(t):n\in\mathbb{N}\}$ is compact for all $t\in T$
conclusions: Then $\{F_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ admits a subsequence, which converges in $\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ pointwise on $T$ to a multifunction $F:T\to\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ such that $\nu_k(F,T)=o(k)$.
nodes.statement_short: Helly-type principle: sequences with $\limsup_n\nu_k(F_n,T)=o(k)$ and pointwise relatively compact values have pointwise convergent subsequences.

We prove only item (a), item (b) being proved similarly with corresponding modifications (`to the left'). We divide the proof into six steps for clarity. Recall that $a=\inf T\in T$, and we set $b:=\sup T$. In the first four steps, we prove the theorem in the case when $t_0=a$ and $b\in T$ (so that $T\subset[t_0,b]$ is bounded), in step~5---when $t_0=a$ and $b
otin T$, and in step~6---when $t_0\!>\!a$ and $T$ is arbitrary. We employ several ideas from \cite{JMAA,MatSb}, \cite[Sections~5,~10]{Sovae}. \smallbreak {\it Step~1}. nodes.statement_short: Approximate by set-valued step functions built from metric projections along partitions, extract a pointwise limit via the selection principle (Theorem B). Then extend from $t_0=a$, $b\in T$ to $b\notin T$ and $t_0>a$ by gluing.

nodes.name: Excess continuity from the left on $T_F$ (e:FsFt)
nodes.statement: \mbox{if $t\in T_F$, then $e(F(s),F(t))\to0$ as $T\ni s\to t-0$.}
nodes.label: e:FsFt

nodes.name: Ordered partitions $\pi_n$ (e:op), (e:noN)
nodes.statement: &\mbox{$t_0=t_0^n<t_1^n<\dots<t_{n-1}^n<t_n^n=b$, \,and}&\\[2pt] &\mbox{$\forall\,t\in S$ $\exists\,n_0=n_0(t)\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $t\in\pi_n$ for all $n\ge n_0$.}&
nodes.label: e:op

nodes.name: Existence of a compact subset at excess distance (e:proj)
nodes.statement: \mbox{there is $Y'\in\mbox{c}(M)$ such that $Y'\subset Y$ and $d_H(X,Y')\le e(X,Y)$.}
nodes.label: e:proj

nodes.name: Metric projection (e:Pr)
nodes.statement: Y'=\mbox{\rm Pr}_Y X:=\{y\in Y:\mbox{there is $x\in X$ such that $d(x,y)=d(x,Y)$}\}.
nodes.label: e:Pr

nodes.name: Step bound (e:Yin)

nodes.label: e:4+

nodes.label: e:gn

nodes.statement: \Gamma_n(t)=\Gamma_n(t_i^n)=Y_i^n\subset F(t_i^n)=F(t)\quad \mbox{for all \,$n\ge n_0$.}
nodes.label: e:Gat

nodes.label: e:*7

nodes.label: e:ijkn

nodes.label: e:Fikn

nodes.label: e:pkt

nodes.name: Plan of proof
nodes.statement: We prove only item (a), item (b) being proved similarly with corresponding modifications (`to the left'). We divide the proof into six steps for clarity. Recall that $a=\inf T\in T$, and we set $b:=\sup T$. In the first four steps, we prove the theorem in the case when $t_0=a$ and $b\in T$ (so that $T\subset[t_0,b]$ is bounded), in step~5---when $t_0=a$ and $b\notin T$, and in step~6---when $t_0\!>\!a$ and $T$ is arbitrary. We employ several ideas from \cite{JMAA,MatSb}, \cite[Sections~5,~10]{Sovae}.
nodes.statement_short: Prove (a) only, in three cases: $t_0=a$, $b\in T$; $t_0=a$, $b\notin T$; $t_0>a$.

nodes.name: Step 1: countable dense set and partitions
nodes.statement: {\it Step~1}. Suppose $T\subset[t_0,b]$ and $t_0,b\in T$. Since ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)$ is finite and the variation function of $F$ to the right $\ori{v}:T\to[0,+\infty)$ is nondecreasing on~$T$, the set of its points of discontinuity on $T$ is at most countable. Denote by $T_F$ the set of points $t\in T$, which are left limit points of $T$ such that $\ori{v}(t)=\ori{v}(t-0)$. It follows that $T\setminus T_F$ is at most countable and, by Lemma~\ref{l:jumps}${\rm(\ori{\mbox{\rm a}})}$, \begin{equation} \mbox{if $t\in T_F$, then $e(F(s),F(t))\to0$ as $T\ni s\to t-0$.} \end{equation} Furthermore, the set $T_0$ of left isolated points of $T$ (i.e., $t\in T$ such that $T_{(t-\varepsilon,t)}=\varnothing$ for some $\varepsilon>0$) is also at most countable (in fact, the intervals of ``emptiness from the left'', corresponding to different left isolated points of $T$, are disjoint, and each such interval contains a rational number). Let $Q$ denote an at most countable dense subset of $T$. We set \begin{equation*} S\!:=\{t_0,b\}\cup(T\setminus T_F)\cup T_0\cup Q \end{equation*} and note that $S\subset T$ is dense in $T$ and at most countable. With no loss of generality we may assume that $S$ is countable, say, $S=\{t_i\}_{i=0}^\infty$. Given $n\in\mathbb{N}$, the set $\pi_n=\{t_i\}_{i=0}^{n-1}\cup\{b\}$ is a partition of $T$. Ordering the points in $\pi_n$ in ascending order and denoting the resulting (ordered) partition of $T$ by $\pi_n=\{t_i^n\}_{i=0}^n$, we get \begin{eqnarray} &\mbox{$t_0=t_0^n<t_1^n<\dots<t_{n-1}^n<t_n^n=b$, \,and}&\\[2pt] &\mbox{$\forall\,t\in S$ $\exists\,n_0=n_0(t)\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $t\in\pi_n$ for all $n\ge n_0$.}& \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Build a countable dense set $S$ containing discontinuities and left isolated points, and partitions $\pi_n$ exhausting it.

nodes.name: Step 2: approximating step selectors
nodes.statement: {\it Step~2}. Let us construct an approximating sequence for the desired set-valued selector of $F$. In order to do this, we need the following observation from \cite[assertion (10.2)]{Sovae}: given $X,Y\in\mbox{c}(M)$, \begin{equation} \mbox{there is $Y'\in\mbox{c}(M)$ such that $Y'\subset Y$ and $d_H(X,Y')\le e(X,Y)$.} \end{equation} In fact, it suffices to define $Y'$ as the \emph{metric projection\/} of $X$ onto~$Y$: \begin{equation} Y'=\mbox{\rm Pr}_Y X:=\{y\in Y:\mbox{there is $x\in X$ such that $d(x,y)=d(x,Y)$}\}. \end{equation} First, given $n\in\mathbb{N}$, we define sets $Y_i^n\in\mbox{c}(M)$, $i=0,1,\dots,n$, inductively as follows. Setting $X=X_0$ and $Y=F(t_0)$ in \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:proj})}, we choose $Y_0:=Y'\in\mbox{c}(M)$ such that $Y_0\subset F(t_0)$ and $d_H(X_0,Y_0)\le e(X_0,F(t_0))$. We put $Y_0^n:=Y_0$ (for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$). Now, suppose $i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ and the set $Y_{i-1}^n\in\mbox{c}(M)$ such that $Y_{i-1}^n\subset F(t_{i-1}^n)$ is already chosen. Then, we put $X=Y_{i-1}^n$ and $Y=F(t_i^n)$ in \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:proj})} and pick $Y_i^n:=Y'\in\mbox{c}(M)$ such that $Y_i^n\subset F(t_i^n)$ and \begin{equation} d_H(Y_{i-1}^n,Y_i^n)\le e(Y_{i-1}^n,F(t_i^n))\le e(F(t_{i-1}^n),F(t_i^n)). \end{equation} The approximating sequence $\Gamma_n:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$, $n\in\mathbb{N}$, is defined as a sequence of set-valued step functions of the form (cf. \cite[equation~(10.3)]{Sovae}): \begin{align} \Gamma_n(t_i^n)&:=Y_i^n\quad\mbox{for all \,$i=0,1,\dots,n;$}\\[2pt] \Gamma_n(t)&:=Y_{i-1}^n\,\,\,\mbox{for all $t\in T\cap(t_{i-1}^n,t_i^n)$ and $i=1,\dots,n$} \end{align} (if $T\cap(t_{i-1}^n,t_i^n)=\varnothing$, then $\Gamma_n$ is left undefined on $(t_{i-1}^n,t_i^n)$). Clearly, \begin{equation*} \Gamma_n(t_0)=\Gamma_n(t_0^n)=Y_0^n=Y_0\subset F(t_0)\quad \mbox{for all \,$n\in\mathbb{N}$.} \end{equation*} Moreover, by the additivity of $\mbox{\rm V}$ and \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Yin})}, we have \begin{align} \mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_n,T)&=\sum_{i=1}^n\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_n,T\cap[t_{i-1}^n,t_i^n]) =\sum_{i=1}^n d_H(Y_{i-1}^n,Y_i^n)\nonumber\\ &\le\sum_{i=1}^n e(F(t_{i-1}^n),F(t_i^n))\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T) \quad\mbox{for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$.} \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Inductively choose metric projections $Y_i^n\subset F(t_i^n)$ and define step functions $\Gamma_n$ with $V(\Gamma_n,T)\le\vec V(F,T)$.

nodes.name: Step 3: hypotheses of Theorem B
nodes.statement: {\it Step~3}. Let us show that $\{\Gamma_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ satisfies the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{t:B}. By virtue of \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:gn})}, we get \begin{equation*} \limsup_{n\to\infty}\nu_k(\Gamma_n,T)\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)\quad\mbox{for all \,$k\in\mathbb{N}$,} \end{equation*} and so, condition (a) in Theorem~\ref{t:B} is satisfied. Now, we verify condition~(b). If $t\in S$, then, by \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:noN})}, there is $n_0=n_0(t)\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $t\in\pi_n$ for all $n\ge n_0$. So, for each $n\ge n_0$ there is $i=i(t,n)\in\{0,1,\dots,n\}$ such that $t=t_i^n$. The definition of $\Gamma_n$ implies \begin{equation} \Gamma_n(t)=\Gamma_n(t_i^n)=Y_i^n\subset F(t_i^n)=F(t)\quad \mbox{for all \,$n\ge n_0$.} \end{equation} In other words, $\{\Gamma_n(t)\}_{n=n_0}^\infty\subset\mbox{c}(F(t))$. Since $F(t)$ is a compact subset of $M$, it follows from \cite[II.1.4]{CV} that $\mbox{c}(F(t))$ is a compact subset of $\mbox{c}(M)$, which implies the desired property for $\{F_n(t)\}_{n=1}^\infty$. Suppose now that $t\in T\setminus S$. We have $t\in T_F\cap(t_0,b)$, i.e., by \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:FsFt})}, \begin{equation} e(F(s),F(t))\to0\quad\mbox{as}\quad T_{(t_0,b)}\ni s\to t-0, \end{equation} where $t$ is a left limit point of $T$, and so, there is a sequence $\tau_k\in T$, $\tau_k<t$, $k\in\mathbb{N}$, such that $\tau_k\to t$ as $k\to\infty$. Since $S$ is dense in $T$, given $k\in\mathbb{N}$, there is $s_k\in S$ such that $|s_k-\tau_k|<t-\tau_k$, which implies $s_k<t$, and $s_k\to t$ as $k\to\infty$. From \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:noN})}, for each $k\in\mathbb{N}$ choose a number $n_0(k)\in\mathbb{N}$ (depending also on~$t$) such that $s_k\in\pi_n$ for all $n\ge n_0(k)$. We may assume (arguing inductively) that the sequence $\{n_0(k)\}_{k=1}^\infty$ is strictly increasing. Given $k\in\mathbb{N}$ and $n\ge n_0(k)$, since $s_k\in\pi_n$, there is a number $j(k,n)\in\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$ such that $s_k=t_{j(k,n)}^n$ and, since $s_k<t$, there is (unique) $i(k,n)\in\{j(k,n),\dots,n-1\}$ such that \begin{equation} s_k=t_{j(k,n)}^n\le t_{i(k,n)}^n<t<t_{i(k,n)+1}^n. \end{equation} By \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:4+})}, \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:re})}, and \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:ijkn})}, we find \begin{equation} \Gamma_n(t)=Y_{i(k,n)}^n\subset F(t_{i(k,n)}^n)\quad\mbox{for all \,$k\in\mathbb{N}$ \,and \,$n\ge n_0(k)$.} \end{equation} Setting $n:=n_0(k)$ and $p_k:=t_{i(k,n_0(k))}^{n_0(k)}$ in \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Fikn})}, we have $\Gamma_{n_0(k)}(t)\subset F(p_k)$ for all $k\in\mathbb{N}$, where, by virtue of \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:ijkn})} and property $s_k\to t$ as $k\to\infty$, \begin{equation} \mbox{$p_k<t$ \,and \,$p_k\to t$ \,as \,$k\to\infty$.} \end{equation} Applying \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:proj})}, for each $k\in\mathbb{N}$ pick $Y_k(t)\in\mbox{c}(M)$ such that $Y_k(t)\subset F(t)$ and \begin{equation} d_H(\Gamma_{n_0(k)},Y_k(t))\le e(\Gamma_{n_0(k)},F(t))\le e(F(p_k),F(t)). \end{equation} It follows from \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:*7})} and \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:pkt})} that the right-hand side in \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Gok})} tends to zero as $k\to\infty$. By the compactness of $\mbox{c}(F(t))$, we may assume (passing to a subsequence of $\{Y_k(t)\}_{k=1}^\infty$ if necessary) that $d_H(Y_k(t),Y(t))\to0$ as $k\to\infty$ for some $Y(t)\in\mbox{c}(M)$ such that $Y(t)\subset F(t)$. Thus, \begin{equation*} d_H(\Gamma_{n_0(k)}(t),Y(t))\!\le\! d_H(\Gamma_{n_0(k)}(t),Y_k(t)) \!+\!d_H(Y_k(t),Y(t))\!\to\!0\quad\mbox{as \,$k\!\to\!\infty$,} \end{equation*} and so, (a subsequence of) the subsequence $\{\Gamma_{n_0(k)}\}_{k=1}^\infty$ of $\{\Gamma_n(t)\}_{n=1}^\infty$ converges in $\mbox{c}(M)$. This finishes the proof of compactness of $\ov{\{\Gamma_n(t)\}_{n=1}^\infty}$ (the closure being taken in $\mbox{c}(M)$).
nodes.statement_short: Verify conditions (a) and (b) of Theorem B for $\{\Gamma_n\}$.

nodes.name: Condition (a)
nodes.statement: By virtue of \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:gn})}, we get \begin{equation*} \limsup_{n\to\infty}\nu_k(\Gamma_n,T)\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)\quad\mbox{for all \,$k\in\mathbb{N}$,} \end{equation*} and so, condition (a) in Theorem~\ref{t:B} is satisfied. Now, we verify condition~(b).
nodes.statement_short: Uniform variation bound gives condition (a).

nodes.name: Condition (b) for $t\in S$
nodes.statement: If $t\in S$, then, by \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:noN})}, there is $n_0=n_0(t)\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $t\in\pi_n$ for all $n\ge n_0$. So, for each $n\ge n_0$ there is $i=i(t,n)\in\{0,1,\dots,n\}$ such that $t=t_i^n$. The definition of $\Gamma_n$ implies \begin{equation} \Gamma_n(t)=\Gamma_n(t_i^n)=Y_i^n\subset F(t_i^n)=F(t)\quad \mbox{for all \,$n\ge n_0$.} \end{equation} In other words, $\{\Gamma_n(t)\}_{n=n_0}^\infty\subset\mbox{c}(F(t))$. Since $F(t)$ is a compact subset of $M$, it follows from \cite[II.1.4]{CV} that $\mbox{c}(F(t))$ is a compact subset of $\mbox{c}(M)$, which implies the desired property for $\{F_n(t)\}_{n=1}^\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Values eventually lie in compact $F(t)$, so c$(F(t))$ is compact.

nodes.name: Condition (b) for $t\notin S$
nodes.statement: Suppose now that $t\in T\setminus S$. We have $t\in T_F\cap(t_0,b)$, i.e., by \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:FsFt})}, \begin{equation} e(F(s),F(t))\to0\quad\mbox{as}\quad T_{(t_0,b)}\ni s\to t-0, \end{equation} where $t$ is a left limit point of $T$, and so, there is a sequence $\tau_k\in T$, $\tau_k<t$, $k\in\mathbb{N}$, such that $\tau_k\to t$ as $k\to\infty$. Since $S$ is dense in $T$, given $k\in\mathbb{N}$, there is $s_k\in S$ such that $|s_k-\tau_k|<t-\tau_k$, which implies $s_k<t$, and $s_k\to t$ as $k\to\infty$. From \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:noN})}, for each $k\in\mathbb{N}$ choose a number $n_0(k)\in\mathbb{N}$ (depending also on~$t$) such that $s_k\in\pi_n$ for all $n\ge n_0(k)$. We may assume (arguing inductively) that the sequence $\{n_0(k)\}_{k=1}^\infty$ is strictly increasing. Given $k\in\mathbb{N}$ and $n\ge n_0(k)$, since $s_k\in\pi_n$, there is a number $j(k,n)\in\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$ such that $s_k=t_{j(k,n)}^n$ and, since $s_k<t$, there is (unique) $i(k,n)\in\{j(k,n),\dots,n-1\}$ such that \begin{equation} s_k=t_{j(k,n)}^n\le t_{i(k,n)}^n<t<t_{i(k,n)+1}^n. \end{equation} By \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:4+})}, \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:re})}, and \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:ijkn})}, we find \begin{equation} \Gamma_n(t)=Y_{i(k,n)}^n\subset F(t_{i(k,n)}^n)\quad\mbox{for all \,$k\in\mathbb{N}$ \,and \,$n\ge n_0(k)$.} \end{equation} Setting $n:=n_0(k)$ and $p_k:=t_{i(k,n_0(k))}^{n_0(k)}$ in \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Fikn})}, we have $\Gamma_{n_0(k)}(t)\subset F(p_k)$ for all $k\in\mathbb{N}$, where, by virtue of \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:ijkn})} and property $s_k\to t$ as $k\to\infty$, \begin{equation} \mbox{$p_k<t$ \,and \,$p_k\to t$ \,as \,$k\to\infty$.} \end{equation} Applying \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:proj})}, for each $k\in\mathbb{N}$ pick $Y_k(t)\in\mbox{c}(M)$ such that $Y_k(t)\subset F(t)$ and \begin{equation} d_H(\Gamma_{n_0(k)},Y_k(t))\le e(\Gamma_{n_0(k)},F(t))\le e(F(p_k),F(t)). \end{equation} It follows from \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:*7})} and \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:pkt})} that the right-hand side in \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Gok})} tends to zero as $k\to\infty$. By the compactness of $\mbox{c}(F(t))$, we may assume (passing to a subsequence of $\{Y_k(t)\}_{k=1}^\infty$ if necessary) that $d_H(Y_k(t),Y(t))\to0$ as $k\to\infty$ for some $Y(t)\in\mbox{c}(M)$ such that $Y(t)\subset F(t)$. Thus, \begin{equation*} d_H(\Gamma_{n_0(k)}(t),Y(t))\!\le\! d_H(\Gamma_{n_0(k)}(t),Y_k(t)) \!+\!d_H(Y_k(t),Y(t))\!\to\!0\quad\mbox{as \,$k\!\to\!\infty$,} \end{equation*} and so, (a subsequence of) the subsequence $\{\Gamma_{n_0(k)}\}_{k=1}^\infty$ of $\{\Gamma_n(t)\}_{n=1}^\infty$ converges in $\mbox{c}(M)$. This finishes the proof of compactness of $\ov{\{\Gamma_n(t)\}_{n=1}^\infty}$ (the closure being taken in $\mbox{c}(M)$).
nodes.statement_short: Approximate $t$ from the left by points of $S$ and project onto $F(t)$ to get a convergent subsequence.

nodes.name: Step 4: limit is a selector with the bounds
nodes.statement: {\it Step~4}. By Theorem~\ref{t:B}, there are a subsequence of $\{\Gamma_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$, which we denote by $\{\Gamma_{l(n)}\}_{n=1}^\infty$ with strictly increasing $l:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$, and a multifunction $\Gamma:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$ such that $d_H(\Gamma_{l(n)}(t),\Gamma(t))\to0$ as $n\to\infty$ for all $t\in T$. Let us show that $\Gamma$ is a set-valued selector of $F$ on $T$. It is clear from \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:4+})} and \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:op})} that $\Gamma(t_0)=Y_0\subset F(t_0)$, and so (cf. Step~2), \begin{equation} d_H(X_0,\Gamma(t_0))\le e(X_0,F(t_0)). \end{equation} If $t\in S$, \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:noN})} implies $t\in\pi_n$ for some $n_0=n_0(t)\in\mathbb{N}$ and all $n\ge n_0$. Since $l(n)\ge l(n_0)\ge n_0$ for $n\ge n_0$, it follows from \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Gat})} that $\Gamma_{l(n)}(t)\subset F(t)$, and so (cf.\ properties (a) and (b) of $e$ in Section~\ref{s:mr}), \begin{align*} e(\Gamma(t),F(t))&\le e(\Gamma(t),\Gamma_{l(n)}(t)) +e(\Gamma_{l(n)}(t),F(t)) \\[2pt] &=e(\Gamma(t),\Gamma_{l(n)}(t))\le d_H(\Gamma(t),\Gamma_{l(n)}(t)) \to0\quad\mbox{as \,$n\to\infty$.} \end{align*} This gives $e(\Gamma(t),F(t))=0$ implying $\Gamma(t)\subset F(t)$. Now suppose that $t\in T\setminus S$. Given $k\in\mathbb{N}$, let $n_0(k)$ be the number (also depending on $t$) from Step~3 such that $s_k\in\pi_n$ for all $n\ge n_0(k)$. Hence, assertions \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:ijkn})} and \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Fikn})} still hold. Setting $n=N(k):=l(n_0(k))\ge n_0(k)$ and $q_k:=t_{i(k,N(k))}^{N(k)}$ in \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:ijkn})} and \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Fikn})}, we find $\Gamma_{N(k)}\subset F(q_k)$, where $q_k<t$, and $q_k\to t$ as $k\to\infty$. For each $k\in\mathbb{N}$, thanks to \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:proj})}, let $Z_k(t)\in\mbox{c}(M)$ be such that $Z_k(t)\subset F(t)$ and \begin{equation*} d_H(\Gamma_{N(k)}(t),Z_k(t))\le e(\Gamma_{N(k)}(t),F(t))\le e(F(q_k),F(t)). \end{equation*} Noting that $e(Z_k(t),F(t))=0$, we get \begin{equation*} e(\Gamma(t),F(t))\le e(\Gamma(t),\Gamma_{N(k)}(t)) +e(\Gamma_{N(k)}(t),Z_k(t))+e(Z_k(t),F(t)) \end{equation*} with the right-hand side tending to zero as $n\!\to\!\infty$. Hence \mbox{$e(\Gamma(t),F(t))\!=\!0$}, and so, $\Gamma(t)\subset F(t)$. Thus, we have shown that $\Gamma(t)\subset F(t)$ for all $t\in T$. The lower semicontinuity of $\mbox{\rm V}$ and \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:gn})} imply \begin{equation*} \mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T)\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_{l(n)},T)\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T). \end{equation*} Since $T_{[a,t_0)}\!=\!\varnothing$ (recall that $t_0\!=\!a$), $T_{[t_0,+\infty)}\!=\!T_{[t_0,b]}\!=\!T$, and \mbox{$J_a(\Gamma,t_0)\!=\!0$}, this proves Theorem~\ref{t:BV}(a) in the case when $t_0=a$ and $b=\sup T\in T$.
nodes.statement_short: Extract a pointwise limit $\Gamma$, show it is a selector and bound its variation by lower semicontinuity.

nodes.name: Extract pointwise limit
nodes.statement: {\it Step~4}. By Theorem~\ref{t:B}, there are a subsequence of $\{\Gamma_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$, which we denote by $\{\Gamma_{l(n)}\}_{n=1}^\infty$ with strictly increasing $l:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$, and a multifunction $\Gamma:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$ such that $d_H(\Gamma_{l(n)}(t),\Gamma(t))\to0$ as $n\to\infty$ for all $t\in T$.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem B gives a pointwise convergent subsequence.

nodes.name: $\Gamma$ is a set-valued selector
nodes.statement: Let us show that $\Gamma$ is a set-valued selector of $F$ on $T$. It is clear from \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:4+})} and \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:op})} that $\Gamma(t_0)=Y_0\subset F(t_0)$, and so (cf. Step~2), \begin{equation} d_H(X_0,\Gamma(t_0))\le e(X_0,F(t_0)). \end{equation} If $t\in S$, \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:noN})} implies $t\in\pi_n$ for some $n_0=n_0(t)\in\mathbb{N}$ and all $n\ge n_0$. Since $l(n)\ge l(n_0)\ge n_0$ for $n\ge n_0$, it follows from \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Gat})} that $\Gamma_{l(n)}(t)\subset F(t)$, and so (cf.\ properties (a) and (b) of $e$ in Section~\ref{s:mr}), \begin{align*} e(\Gamma(t),F(t))&\le e(\Gamma(t),\Gamma_{l(n)}(t)) +e(\Gamma_{l(n)}(t),F(t)) \\[2pt] &=e(\Gamma(t),\Gamma_{l(n)}(t))\le d_H(\Gamma(t),\Gamma_{l(n)}(t)) \to0\quad\mbox{as \,$n\to\infty$.} \end{align*} This gives $e(\Gamma(t),F(t))=0$ implying $\Gamma(t)\subset F(t)$. Now suppose that $t\in T\setminus S$. Given $k\in\mathbb{N}$, let $n_0(k)$ be the number (also depending on $t$) from Step~3 such that $s_k\in\pi_n$ for all $n\ge n_0(k)$. Hence, assertions \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:ijkn})} and \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Fikn})} still hold. Setting $n=N(k):=l(n_0(k))\ge n_0(k)$ and $q_k:=t_{i(k,N(k))}^{N(k)}$ in \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:ijkn})} and \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Fikn})}, we find $\Gamma_{N(k)}\subset F(q_k)$, where $q_k<t$, and $q_k\to t$ as $k\to\infty$. For each $k\in\mathbb{N}$, thanks to \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:proj})}, let $Z_k(t)\in\mbox{c}(M)$ be such that $Z_k(t)\subset F(t)$ and \begin{equation*} d_H(\Gamma_{N(k)}(t),Z_k(t))\le e(\Gamma_{N(k)}(t),F(t))\le e(F(q_k),F(t)). \end{equation*} Noting that $e(Z_k(t),F(t))=0$, we get \begin{equation*} e(\Gamma(t),F(t))\le e(\Gamma(t),\Gamma_{N(k)}(t)) +e(\Gamma_{N(k)}(t),Z_k(t))+e(Z_k(t),F(t)) \end{equation*} with the right-hand side tending to zero as $n\!\to\!\infty$. Hence \mbox{$e(\Gamma(t),F(t))\!=\!0$}, and so, $\Gamma(t)\subset F(t)$. Thus, we have shown that $\Gamma(t)\subset F(t)$ for all $t\in T$.
nodes.statement_short: Show $\Gamma(t)\subset F(t)$ separately for $t\in S$ and $t\notin S$.

nodes.name: Initial value estimate
nodes.statement: It is clear from \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:4+})} and \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:op})} that $\Gamma(t_0)=Y_0\subset F(t_0)$, and so (cf. Step~2), \begin{equation} d_H(X_0,\Gamma(t_0))\le e(X_0,F(t_0)). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\Gamma(t_0)=Y_0$ gives (e:Xo).

nodes.name: Case $t\in S$
nodes.statement: If $t\in S$, \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:noN})} implies $t\in\pi_n$ for some $n_0=n_0(t)\in\mathbb{N}$ and all $n\ge n_0$. Since $l(n)\ge l(n_0)\ge n_0$ for $n\ge n_0$, it follows from \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Gat})} that $\Gamma_{l(n)}(t)\subset F(t)$, and so (cf.\ properties (a) and (b) of $e$ in Section~\ref{s:mr}), \begin{align*} e(\Gamma(t),F(t))&\le e(\Gamma(t),\Gamma_{l(n)}(t)) +e(\Gamma_{l(n)}(t),F(t)) \\[2pt] &=e(\Gamma(t),\Gamma_{l(n)}(t))\le d_H(\Gamma(t),\Gamma_{l(n)}(t)) \to0\quad\mbox{as \,$n\to\infty$.} \end{align*} This gives $e(\Gamma(t),F(t))=0$ implying $\Gamma(t)\subset F(t)$.
nodes.statement_short: Excess of $\Gamma(t)$ over $F(t)$ vanishes in the limit.

nodes.name: Case $t\notin S$
nodes.statement: Now suppose that $t\in T\setminus S$. Given $k\in\mathbb{N}$, let $n_0(k)$ be the number (also depending on $t$) from Step~3 such that $s_k\in\pi_n$ for all $n\ge n_0(k)$. Hence, assertions \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:ijkn})} and \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Fikn})} still hold. Setting $n=N(k):=l(n_0(k))\ge n_0(k)$ and $q_k:=t_{i(k,N(k))}^{N(k)}$ in \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:ijkn})} and \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Fikn})}, we find $\Gamma_{N(k)}\subset F(q_k)$, where $q_k<t$, and $q_k\to t$ as $k\to\infty$. For each $k\in\mathbb{N}$, thanks to \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:proj})}, let $Z_k(t)\in\mbox{c}(M)$ be such that $Z_k(t)\subset F(t)$ and \begin{equation*} d_H(\Gamma_{N(k)}(t),Z_k(t))\le e(\Gamma_{N(k)}(t),F(t))\le e(F(q_k),F(t)). \end{equation*} Noting that $e(Z_k(t),F(t))=0$, we get \begin{equation*} e(\Gamma(t),F(t))\le e(\Gamma(t),\Gamma_{N(k)}(t)) +e(\Gamma_{N(k)}(t),Z_k(t))+e(Z_k(t),F(t)) \end{equation*} with the right-hand side tending to zero as $n\!\to\!\infty$. Hence \mbox{$e(\Gamma(t),F(t))\!=\!0$}, and so, $\Gamma(t)\subset F(t)$. Thus, we have shown that $\Gamma(t)\subset F(t)$ for all $t\in T$.
nodes.statement_short: Use projections $Z_k(t)\subset F(t)$ and left continuity of the excess.

nodes.name: Variation bound by lower semicontinuity
nodes.statement: The lower semicontinuity of $\mbox{\rm V}$ and \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:gn})} imply \begin{equation*} \mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T)\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_{l(n)},T)\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T). \end{equation*} Since $T_{[a,t_0)}\!=\!\varnothing$ (recall that $t_0\!=\!a$), $T_{[t_0,+\infty)}\!=\!T_{[t_0,b]}\!=\!T$, and \mbox{$J_a(\Gamma,t_0)\!=\!0$}, this proves Theorem~\ref{t:BV}(a) in the case when $t_0=a$ and $b=\sup T\in T$.
nodes.statement_short: Lower semicontinuity of $V$ and (e:gn) give $V(\Gamma,T)\le\vec V(F,T)$.

nodes.name: Remark: exact initial value
nodes.statement: {\it Remark}. Note that if $X_0\subset F(t_0)$, we have, by \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Xo})}, $\Gamma(t_0)=X_0$.
nodes.statement_short: If $X_0\subset F(t_0)$ then $\Gamma(t_0)=X_0$.

nodes.name: Step 5: $b\notin T$
nodes.statement: {\it Step~5}. Suppose $t_0=a$ and $b=\sup T\notin T$, so that $T_{[a,t_0)}\!=\!\varnothing$, $T_{[t_0,+\infty)}\!=\!T$, and $J_a(\Gamma,t_0)=0$. Pick an increasing sequence $\{t_k\}_{k=1}^\infty\subset T$ such that $t_k\to b$ as $k\to\infty$. Noting that ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t_0,t_1]})\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)<+\infty$ and applying Steps 1--4 to $F$ on $T_{[t_0,t_1]}$, we get a set-valued selector $\Gamma_0:T_{[t_0,t_1]}\to\mbox{c}(M)$ of $F$ on $T_{[t_0,t_1]}$ such that \begin{equation*} d_H(X_0,\Gamma_0(t_0))\le e(X_0,F(t_0))\quad\mbox{and}\quad \mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_0,T_{[t_0,t_1]})\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t_0,t_1]}). \end{equation*} Inductively, if $k\in\mathbb{N}$, and a set-valued selector $\Gamma_{k-1}$ of $F$ on $T_{[t_{k-1},t_k]}$ is already chosen, we note that ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t_k,t_{k+1}]})\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)<+\infty$, again apply Steps 1--4, and find a set-valued selector $\Gamma_k$ of $F$ on $T_{[t_k,t_{k+1}]}$ such that $\Gamma_k(t_k)=\Gamma_{k-1}(t_k)$ and $\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_k,T_{[t_k,t_{k+1}]})\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t_k,t_{k+1}]})$. Since $t_k\to b$ as $k\to\infty$, and $b\notin T$, we have $T=\bigcup_{k=0}^\infty T_{[t_k,t_{k+1}]}$, so if $t\in T$ and $t\in T_{[t_k,t_{k+1}]}$ for some $k\in\{0\}\cup\mathbb{N}$, we set $\Gamma(t):=\Gamma_k(t)$. Clearly, $\Gamma:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$ is a well-defined set-valued selector of $F$ on $T$, inequality \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Xo})} holds, and, by \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:ttos})} and the additivity of $\mbox{\rm V}$ and~${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}$, \begin{align*} \mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T)&=\lim_{n\to\infty}\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T_{(-\infty,t_n]}) =\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_k,T_{[t_k,t_{k+1}]})\\ &\le\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t_k,t_{k+1}]}) =\lim_{n\to\infty}{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(-\infty,t_n]})={\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Exhaust $T$ by segments up to $t_k\to b$, apply Steps 1--4 inductively and glue.

nodes.name: Step 6: $t_0>a$
nodes.statement:

Since ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{m V}}}(F,T_{[a,t_0)})$ and ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{m V}}}(F,T_{[t_0,+\infty)})$ do not exceed ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{m V}}}(F,T)<+\infty$, and $X_0\in\mbox{c}(M)$, we apply Steps 1--5 twice: first, to $F$ on $T_{[a,t_0)}$ with arbitrary $K_0\in\mbox{c}(M)$ in order to obtain a set-valued selector $\Gamma_1$ of $F$ on $T_{[a,t_0)}$ such that  egin{equation*} d_H(K_0,\Gamma_1(a))\le e(K_0,F(a))\quad\mbox{and}\quad \mbox{m V}(\Gamma_1,T_{[a,t_0)})\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{m V}}}(F,T_{[a,t_0)}), \end{equation*} and, second, to $F$ on $T_{[t_0,+\infty)}$ in order to obtain a set-valued selector $\Gamma_2$ of $F$ on $T_{[t_0,+\infty)}$ such that  egin{equation*} d_H(X_0,\Gamma_2(t_0))\le e(X_0,F(t_0))\quad\mbox{and}\quad \mbox{m V}(\Gamma_2,T_{[t_0,+\infty)})\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{m V}}}(F,T_{[t_0,+\infty)}). \end{equation*} Given $t\in T$, we set $\Gamma(t):=\Gamma_1(t)$ if $t\in T_{[a,t_0)}$, and $\Gamma(t):=\Gamma_2(t)$ if $t\in T_{[t_0,+\infty)}$. \linebreak Clearly, $\Gamma:T	o\mbox{c}(M)$ is a set-valued selector of $F$ on $T$, inequality \mbox{m(ef{e:Xo})} holds, $\mbox{m V}(\Gamma,T_{[a,t_0)})\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{m V}}}(F,T_{[a,t_0)})$, and $\mbox{m V}(\Gamma,T_{[t_0,+\infty)})\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{m V}}}(F,T_{[t_0,+\infty)})$. nodes.statement_short: Glue selectors on $T_{[a,t_0)}$ and $T_{[t_0,\infty)}$ and bound the variation with the jump term $J_a$.

nodes.name: Apply Steps 1--5 on both sides
nodes.statement: {\it Step~6}. Finally, suppose $t_0>a$. Since ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[a,t_0)})$ and ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t_0,+\infty)})$ do not exceed ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)<+\infty$, and $X_0\in\mbox{c}(M)$, we apply Steps 1--5 twice: first, to $F$ on $T_{[a,t_0)}$ with arbitrary $K_0\in\mbox{c}(M)$ in order to obtain a set-valued selector $\Gamma_1$ of $F$ on $T_{[a,t_0)}$ such that \begin{equation*} d_H(K_0,\Gamma_1(a))\le e(K_0,F(a))\quad\mbox{and}\quad \mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_1,T_{[a,t_0)})\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[a,t_0)}), \end{equation*} and, second, to $F$ on $T_{[t_0,+\infty)}$ in order to obtain a set-valued selector $\Gamma_2$ of $F$ on $T_{[t_0,+\infty)}$ such that \begin{equation*} d_H(X_0,\Gamma_2(t_0))\le e(X_0,F(t_0))\quad\mbox{and}\quad \mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_2,T_{[t_0,+\infty)})\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t_0,+\infty)}). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Selectors $\Gamma_1$ on $T_{[a,t_0)}$ and $\Gamma_2$ on $T_{[t_0,\infty)}$.

nodes.name: Glue and second inequality
nodes.statement: Given $t\in T$, we set $\Gamma(t):=\Gamma_1(t)$ if $t\in T_{[a,t_0)}$, and $\Gamma(t):=\Gamma_2(t)$ if $t\in T_{[t_0,+\infty)}$. \linebreak Clearly, $\Gamma:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$ is a set-valued selector of $F$ on $T$, inequality \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Xo})} holds, $\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T_{[a,t_0)})\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[a,t_0)})$, and $\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T_{[t_0,+\infty)})\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t_0,+\infty)})$. Furthermore, since ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}$ is additive, the second inequality in \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:s1t0})} holds (recall that $a=\min T$): \begin{align*} {\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[a,t_0)})+{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t_0,+\infty)})&\le {\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[a,t_0]})+{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t_0,+\infty)})=\\[2pt] &={\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[a,+\infty)})={\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Define $\Gamma$ piecewise; additivity of $\vec V$ gives the second inequality of (e:s1t0).

nodes.name: First inequality in (e:s1t0)
nodes.statement:
Let us prove the first inequality in \mbox{m(ef{e:s1t0})}. Suppose $s_0\in T_{[a,t_0)}$. Hence $s_0=\max T_{[a,t_0)}<t_0$, and so, $T_{[a,t_0)}=T_{[a,s_0]}$ and $T_{[s_0,t_0]}=\{s_0,t_0\}$ (two-point set). e\varnothing$ (and a fortiori $T\cap(s_0-\varepsilon,s_0)
e\varnothing$). Let us show that the limit in the right-hand side of \mbox{m(ef{e:J})} exists in $[0,+\infty)$. otin T_{[a,t_0)}$ implies $T_{[a,s_0)}=T_{[a,t_0)}$, by virtue of \mbox{m(ef{e:ttos})}, the limit of the first term in \mbox{m(ef{e:star})} as $T
